gates.title: Mail: choose hourly digest or simpler throttle
gates.body: Investigation for run 916ed2c55328491b8f73316a8f630b73: nine sent SMTP receipts in .tmp/evening-loop-20261120/notifications between 2026-11-20 14:40:43 and 17:55:50 UTC; each corresponding event receipt records attempts=1. These are distinct WORKING milestone/push/eval messages, including sends at 15:16:58 and 15:19:01. scripts/loop_notify.py sends each invocation immediately with no cadence guard. Dashboard terminal mail independently deduplicates only run-id/status, not overall frequency. ADR-090 explicitly defers digest batching. Decision needed: delivery policy and durable aggregation. A: One hourly digest of routine updates using existing dashboard records/supervision scheduling, with durable delivery progress and all notification producers coordinated. Pros: preserves intermediate updates, flushes after quiet periods, survives restarts; no separate service needed. Cons: adds persisted delivery state and aggregation/recovery logic; depends on scheduler availability. B: Hourly send-time throttle using existing receipts, with the dashboard retaining detail. Pros: smaller change, no separate queue or timer. Cons: suppressed details are absent from mail and no final flush occurs without a later event. Recommendation: A, default 60 minutes (within the requested one-to-two-hour cadence). Proposed exceptions: first actionable blocker and final sleep/closeout immediate, deduplicated; routine completions remain batched. Exceptions are pending owner choice, not approved policy. Question: A or B, and should actionable blockers/final closeout bypass the hourly limit, or should all mail wait? Implementation pending; no cadence fix is claimed.
options: A: Hourly digest; confirm exception policy
B: Hourly throttle; confirm exception policy

gates.title: Family-5 G3: local full gates, affected selection, or CI spike?
gates.body: Decision needed: gate/CI direction after Family-5. G1 excludes scratch fingerprints; G2's eight-worker trial is red and does not justify changing the serial gate. Historical affected-selection includes 3/3 sampled historical failure modules plus one new regression module, using fixing diffs and today's manifest, not historical failure replay; that biased sample is insufficient for adoption. Details: docs/test-workflow.md, Family-5 follow-up. A: Keep serial full gates and collect prospective affected-selection shadow evidence. Pro: preserves coverage, no new service/access boundary. Con: retains full gate cost and needs more comparisons. B: Adopt affected pre-push selection while retaining a mandatory full suite before merge. Pro: fewer repeated tests. Con: incomplete dependency knowledge can miss failures, evidence is limited, and merge enforcement must be specified. C: Authorize a GitHub Actions design spike, with hosted versus isolated self-hosted runner boundaries decided before setup. Pro: independent reporting and execution history. Con: clean checkouts lack local assets; hosted execution changes data/access boundaries, while owner-PC runners retain contention and execute workflow code on that PC. Jenkins offers control but adds controller/service maintenance; defer without a distinct requirement. Recommendation: A until prospective recall and clean-checkout evidence support adoption. No hook change, runner installation, credentials, paid usage or scheduling is authorized by this brief. Question: A, B, or C, and what constraint drives your choice?
options: A: Retain full gates; evaluate shadow selection
B: Adopt affected push checks plus full merge gate
C: Authorize GitHub Actions design spike

gates.title: Eval allowance budgets: strict cap or observed stop threshold?
gates.body: B is accepted from source bd5fa3a29bb143669ea084f5ef49f218: full evaluation scope with 10% per allowance bucket/cycle. Decision needed: how to enforce that cap when a provider exposes percentage usage/reset observations but no guaranteed per-request allowance charge. Why it matters: checking after a call can detect an overshoot only after consumption; concurrent product calls and delayed readings also make attribution uncertain. A: Keep a strict cap and fail closed on routes without a defensible pre-call upper bound; continue local harness/planner and grade storage independently. Pro: preserves the approved ceiling and product headroom. Con: some allowance routes remain unevaluated until a usable bound exists. B: Treat 10% as an observed stop threshold, with sequential bounded calls and fresh readings before/after each call; stop on missing/stale readings or threshold crossing. Pro: permits sampling percentage-only providers. Con: a call or reporting delay can overshoot 10%, and shared product consumption cannot reliably be separated. Recommendation: A, because B changes the approved allowance boundary. This does not reopen full-scope approval or authorize metered spend. Question: A (strict cap with unsupported routes deferred), or B (accept the overshoot risk of an observed threshold)?
options: A: Strict cap; defer routes without bounds
B: Observed threshold; accept overshoot risk

Decision needed: create the read-only service account so the dashboard can read Go usage windows.

Why it matters: the .env key is the Go INFERENCE key, proven 403 on all usage endpoints (2026-11-17). Only a console service-account key (or a browser-cookie session) can read the 5h/weekly/monthly windows. Extra Usage is OFF, so headroom reads literally once wired.

Steps (verified against dev.opencode.ai/docs/console/api):
1. Console > Settings > Service accounts > Add Service Account, name e.g. workbench-usage.
2. Open it > Add API Key, name e.g. usage-read.
3. Permissions: Restricted with Usage set to Read (tightest), or Read only. Expiry: Never (or 365d custom + rotation note).
4. Copy the key ONCE (shown once, oc_sk_... prefix afterwards).

Then paste it here as your answer (or add OPENCODE_USAGE_KEY=<key> to .env yourself). Do NOT overwrite OPENCODE_API_KEY. Read-only keys cannot call models; usage counts to the service account's own budget; revocable anytime.

Technical recommendation: Restricted + Usage/Read + Never expiry.
Question: paste the key, or say cookie-path.

gates.title: Worktree OS isolation: select the first backend prototype
gates.body: Decision needed: choose the backend feasibility prototype for approved provider-neutral OS isolation (source bedd17b747a64506ad8358541c660cc5, ADR-095). B selected the direction; its brief explicitly left technology and costs for selection. Why it matters: the backend determines Windows tool/client compatibility, credential access, host-output mediation and ongoing infrastructure. A: Windows AppContainer prototype. Pro: preserves native Windows tools without a guest installation; OS token/ACL isolation. Con: custom Windows launcher/ACL/handle lifecycle work; client authentication, network and tool compatibility remain unproven. B: VM-based worker design/prototype. Pro: separate kernel and explicit sharing. Con: guest toolchain/auth provisioning, memory/startup and lifecycle cost; Linux changes Windows tooling, Windows guests need backend/licensing selection. Technical recommendation: A as a bounded synthetic local feasibility prototype, with no provider calls, broad profile/key grants or machine-wide privilege changes. Prove ordinary coding and negative host-write tests before production integration; report incompatibility rather than weakening containment. No backend has been installed or selected. Question: A or B, and what is the main reason for your choice? Source remains answered/open; enforcement and its proving checks are INCOMPLETE.

gates.title: Host-side proxy: filtered direct connection or isolated-network relay?
gates.body:
Decision needed: connection containment for the accepted B host-side inference proxy (source 98654698af0b458492b0bb74ddd3c5e3). B remains accepted; this does not reopen container versus host deployment.
Why it matters: the proven internal/isolated worker network blocks host listeners. Host-gateway address mapping does not itself restrict destination ports. Bearer authentication protects the inference endpoint, not other host services. Native host-side containment has not been proved.
D: Filtered direct host connection. Pro: direct HTTP follows the original brief and avoids a relay. Con: platform-specific filtering, potentially privileged setup and rollback, plus IPv4/IPv6 bypass proof; hostname mapping alone is insufficient.
R: Host-initiated relay on the isolated worker network. Pro: preserves worker isolation from host listeners while keeping provider credentials/admission on the host. Con: adds a relay protocol/component and bounded mediation, cancellation and cleanup work; exact transport needs design.
Technical recommendation: R, because it preserves the proved worker network and avoids relying on new host-wide filtering. This recommendation is not an owner decision.
Question: approve R, or select D with network-policy setup scope? What constraint drives the choice?
AI next: implement the selected connection, prove positive synthetic inference and negative host/public/DNS/foreign-run access and lifecycle cleanup, then perform separately admitted provider acceptance. Keep source 98654698 open until proved. See docs/decisions/ADR-095-provider-neutral-worktree-write-isolation.md, host-side section.
Instruction audit: AGENTS.md and docs/workflow.md already require each option's pros AND cons and a recommendation. The original brief failed those rules; file-brief.py validates option count, not semantic completeness.
